# Part 3 source records: first sweep (11 lanes)

**Date:** 2026-09-29 · generated by `tools/evidence-check/build_part3_files.py` from the verified store; not edited by hand.

Each work was saved as full text and read by one agent, which locked every item to a line of the saved text with a short verbatim anchor. A script checked that each anchor occurs in the saved text and that the numbers of the item stand within three lines of it. A second agent, which did not write the record, then tried to refute each item against the text. Items shown here passed both checks. Where the auditor corrected an item, the corrected wording is shown and the Audit column says so. The verbatim anchors and the saved texts are kept outside the repository; this file gives the location of every item instead. Only works that are eligible under the source rule of 2026-09-29 (D313) are listed; the others are in the evidence ledger, section 1b.

Columns: # = item index (the reference is <record id>#<index>); Field = what the item is about; Line = line in the saved text of the version read. Full references: evidence ledger, References.

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | result | From interviews with RPA project leaders at a hospital and a large B2B enterprise, the authors summarise that RPA adoption was held back by high set-up costs (12-18 months), unreliable execution (60% initial accuracy) and burdensome maintenance (multiple FTEs). The 12-18 months combines the B2B case (over 12 months from vendor contract to production deployment, Sec. 3.2 line 115) and the hospital case (about 18 months, a leadership estimate, Sec. 3.1 line 110). The 60% initial accuracy is given in detail only for the B2B case (line 116). The Sec. 3 intro (line 107) attributes 'accuracies started around 60% and peaked at 95%' to both organisations jointly, but Sec. 3.1 reports no accuracy figure for the hospital. 'Multiple FTEs' rests on the B2B case's 2 monitoring FTEs (line 117). | 12-18 months; 60% initial accuracy; multiple FTEs | Interview-reported figures from two organisations (hospital revenue-cycle management; B2B invoice processing), not measured by the authors. Set-up = time from project start (B2B: initial vendor contract) to deployment of the RPA bot. RPA-bot 'accuracy' is not defined in the text. FTE = full-time equivalent staff. | Abstract | 66 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | loop_cost | B2B case: the RPA bot was 60% accurate right after deployment and took 6 months of iteration to reach a final accuracy of 95% (Sec. 3.2 line 116; Sec. 1 line 78 says '6 months of improvement'). This is the RPA bot's improvement period, not ECLAIR's. The paper does not say who carried out the iteration. That it was a human-run fix loop is our inference from RPA bots being hand-coded rule sets (line 102). | 60% initial -> 95% final after 6 months of iteration | Reported by the enterprise's head of revenue operations in an interview (Sec. 3.2 line 114), for a single invoice-processing workflow. 'Accuracy' is not defined (per invoice or otherwise). 6 months is calendar time, not effort. No count of iterations or runs is given. | Sec. 3.2 B2B Enterprise Invoice Processing, (2) Brittle Execution | 116 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | human_in_loop | B2B case: because a wrongly processed invoice is costly, 2 FTEs were assigned to monitor the deployed RPA bot continuously - debugging issues, adding new input formats and inspecting outputs - and an outside firm also did manual batch reviews. | 2 FTEs | Staffing reported in interview; FTE = full-time equivalent; ongoing maintenance after deployment, not set-up. | Sec. 3.2, (3) Burdensome Maintenance | 117 | primary | supported |
| 3 | mechanism | ECLAIR applies multimodal foundation models to the three stages of traditional RPA: Demonstrate (learn a workflow from video demonstrations and written documentation), Execute (observe the GUI and plan actions), Validate (self-monitor and error-correct) (lines 85-89). | - | Definitional statement of the system design; no measurement. | Sec. 1 Introduction | 83 | primary | supported |
| 4 | what_is_changed | ECLAIR is designed to learn from passively collected human demonstrations with no updates to the underlying FM's weights (line 122). In Demonstrate, GPT-4 writes an SOP from a demonstration (Sec. 4.1.1, line 126). In Execute, an SOP is given to GPT-4 as input when it suggests the next action (line 171). The paper does not state that the Execute experiments used the GPT-4-generated SOPs (annotators also wrote SOPs, line 120); the stages are evaluated separately. | - | Design statement ('aims to'); no measurement. | Sec. 4.1 Demonstrate | 122 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | result | SOPs that GPT-4 writes from the workflow description + key-frame screenshots + click/keystroke log (WD+KF+ACT) are judged sufficient to complete 93% of workflows; with screenshots only (WD+KF) 90%, but with almost twice as many hallucinated steps (1.05 vs 0.57 incorrect steps per SOP). | 93% (WD+KF+ACT); 90% (WD+KF) | 30 WebArena workflows (Gitlab and Magento) that the WebArena GPT-4 baseline had failed (line 120); GPT-4 generates an SOP; a human annotator, using a manually written SOP as reference, judges 'correctness' = whether following the generated SOP completes the workflow (Sec. 4.1.1 Set-Up, line 126; Table 1). Not an agent execution result. | Sec. 4.1.1 Takeaways; Table 1 | 165 | primary | supported |
| 6 | result | Giving GPT-4 the SOP raises next-action suggestion accuracy from 0.83 to 0.92 and overall workflow completion accuracy from 0.17 to 0.40 on the 30 workflows (text: 'up to 23 points', line 186; 'doubles', line 167). For next-action suggestion the model gets the ground-truth action history at every step (line 171). The paper does not say how overall completion was computed, or whether it came from a free-running run, and the abstract and intro call the 40% an 'end-to-end completion rate' (lines 66, 87). | completion 0.17 -> 0.40; next-action acc. 0.83 -> 0.92 | 30 WebArena workflows (Gitlab, Magento) chosen because the WebArena GPT-4 baseline failed them (line 120). Next-action suggestion accuracy: at each step GPT-4 gets the ground-truth action history, full SOP and current GUI, and a human annotator judges whether the suggestion is semantically equivalent to the ground-truth action (line 171). Overall Workflow Completion Acc.: not defined, beyond the note that the model must also ground its actions to complete the workflow (line 186). The text does not say whether ground-truth history was supplied for it or who judged completion. No cost, time or step counts are reported. | Sec. 4.2.1; Table 2 (rows without / with SOP) | 179 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 7 | signal | As a candidate runtime success signal, GPT-4 judges from a trace plus workflow description whether the workflow was completed: precision 0.90, recall 0.84, F1 0.87. Negatives are real traces truncated by a random number of frames (line 260), not genuine agent failures. Step-level integrity-constraint checking is much weaker (F1 0.47, line 244-247). | precision 0.90, recall 0.84, F-score 0.87 | Binary classification by GPT-4 over full human-demonstration traces (positives) vs truncated traces (negatives) from the 30-workflow dataset; metrics averaged across the 30 workflows (Table 4 caption, line 235). | Sec. 4.3.2; Table 4 row 'Workflow Completion' | 248 | primary | supported |
| 8 | proposal_method | Self-improvement is only proposed, not implemented: as ECLAIR repeatedly executes a workflow it could document the observed effects of its actions and compile a database of reusable 'skills', possibly following self-driving-database principles (continuously applying configuration 'actions' based on utilisation patterns). | - | Discussion proposal; no experiment. | Sec. 5 Discussion, 'Self-Improvement' | 267 | primary | supported |
| 9 | limitation | The authors call the SOP-guided 40% end-to-end completion rate 'still far from the accuracy needed for enterprise settings' (line 87). The 0% comparison point is the WebArena GPT-4 baseline on tasks selected because it failed them (line 120), whereas the paper's own no-SOP condition in Table 2 scored 0.17. | 0% to 40%; 30 tasks | Table 2 'Overall Workflow Completion Acc.' with SOP (0.40) on 30 WebArena Gitlab/Magento tasks. How completion was computed (free-running or with the ground-truth action history, and who judged it) is not stated in the text. The 0% is the WebArena GPT-4 baseline's result on these tasks, which were chosen because it failed them. | Sec. 1 Introduction, item (2) Execute | 87 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
